strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: the action space of insertion-based variable-length discrete flow models is much larger than fixed-length masked diffusion, so learning a good generation order is a natural way to improve training and sampling.

Provides a nontrivial theoretical construction: it uses projected discrete flow matching to define learnable per-position target rates, proves in Proposition 1 that the proposed insertion/unmasking rates generate the desired per-position marginals, and derives a projected rate-matching objective.

The Kumaraswamy parameterization is a clever design choice: with a_in = a_um = a, it yields closed-form hazards and inverse-CDF sampling, enabling training without simulating the full CTMC trajectory and with a single backward pass per example via a REINFORCE leave-one-out estimator.

The star-graph traversal experiments provide compelling evidence that learned insertion order can recover a known locally optimal order: on hard star graphs, LFlexMDM with fixed b_um and confidence selection reaches 87.9-88.1% exact match, compared to 6.0-7.4% for FlexMDM, 23.0% for ARM, and 21.0% for MDM. The correlation analysis (-0.91 vs -0.22/-0.60) supports the claim that the model learns to generate from arm endpoints toward the junction.

The molecule generation results show improvements in validity and quality under nucleus sampling, e.g., at p=0.5 validity 99.7% vs 98.9% and quality 54.7% vs 39.5%, and the quality-diversity trade-off curves suggest LFlexMDM can dominate FlexMDM at comparable diversity.

The paper explores several relevant design choices, including shared vs. separate backbones, frozen vs. trainable target unmasking rates, confidence-based unmasking, and nucleus sampling. It honestly reports that fully trainable b_um destabilizes training and that shared backbones underperform on the hard graph task.
The proposed method is a natural extension of FlexMDM and is placed within the broader discrete flow matching framework, with a sampling algorithm based on tau-leaping and nucleus sampling.

The work has potential practical significance for domains where variable-length generation order matters, especially molecular design and graph-based reasoning, and the learned order dynamics may reduce the need for hand-designed generation heuristics.
weaknesses: The central claim of learning full order dynamics is overstated. Only the target insertion rate b_in is trained; the target unmasking rate is fixed to b_um=1 because trainable b_um destabilizes training. Unmasking order is therefore not learned as a target distribution but is handled by inference-time confidence-based selection. The title and abstract imply joint insertion/unmasking order learning, which is not actually delivered.

The empirical evaluation is narrow: only star-graph traversal and small-molecule generation are considered. There is no comparison to other insertion-based or order-learning baselines such as EditFlows, Insertion Language Models, or Wang et al. (2025), despite these being the most relevant prior work. The claim that there have been 'limited attempts' to learn generation order in insertion-based models is not fully supported given prior work by Gu et al. (2019), Brantley et al. (2019), and Wang et al. (2025).

The molecule-generation improvements are not clearly attributable to learned order dynamics alone. At p=1.0, validity and quality are essentially the same as FlexMDM (98.9 vs. 98.9 and 39.6 vs. 39.5). The reported gains arise when using nucleus sampling and confidence-based unmasking, which are inference-time modifications. FlexMDM is not shown with the same sampling-time tuning, so the comparison is not controlled.

There is a text/figure inconsistency in the molecule analysis: the main text says Figure 7 (right) varies the nucleus sampling p cutoff, but the figure legend refers to steps=128/1024. This makes it unclear whether the quality-diversity trade-off is driven by order learning, sampling steps, or nucleus truncation.

Reproducibility is weak. There is no working code link (only a project placeholder), no dataset splits, no definitions of the molecule metrics (validity, uniqueness, diversity, quality), no model sizes for the auxiliary rate network ('medium', 'small', 'xtiny'), no compute budget, and no seeds for the graph-traversal experiments. Several hyperparameters (batch size, regularization weights, number of grid points K, architecture details) are missing or only partially specified.

Presentation quality is poor and impedes understanding. There are numerous typos ('tokens is are', 'the the', 'simultaneous simultaneous', 'LMFlexMDM', 'LNFlexMDM'), Table 1 and Table 2 are misaligned or missing values, and several equations contain inconsistent notation (e.g., Eq. 11 uses δ_{|H|} where δ_[M] is intended; Eq. 81 uses z1^i where z1^{s_t^i} is needed; Eq. 88 again uses δ_[H]). Figure 1's caption uses λ_m while the main text uses λ_in, and the roles of K^θ, λ^θ, and the auxiliary φ network are not always clear.

The theoretical derivation is not fully convincing. Appendix D.4 contains index inconsistencies and the loss terms in Eq. 11 are hard to verify against the projected rate-matching derivation. The claim of a single backward pass is empirical, with no variance analysis of the REINFORCE leave-one-out estimator, which is known to be high variance. Schedule regularization is a heuristic that is not ablated, and its effect on the learned order is unknown.

Fixing b_um=1 is an unprincipled workaround for training instability. The paper does not explain why trainable b_um destabilizes training or whether the instability can be fixed with better parameterization, regularization, or variance reduction. This limits the generality of the proposed 'learnable order dynamics'.

The target rate network φ sees the clean sequence z1 and predicts per-token rates. This provides a strong auxiliary supervised signal, but there is no parameter-matched comparison to FlexMDM with extra capacity. The shared-backbone experiment performs much worse on the hard graph task (34.2% vs. 87.9%), suggesting that a separate auxiliary transformer is doing substantial work, yet its computational cost is not reported.

The paper lacks a limitations section. The impact statement is generic and does not discuss dual-use concerns for molecule generation, computational overhead, failure modes, or cases where learned order might harm diversity. The future-work discussion is vague ('room for further improvement').

Statistical rigor is limited. The graph-traversal results in Table 1 are reported without error bars or multiple seeds. The molecule results have error bars over sampled molecules but not necessarily over training seeds, and no significance tests are provided. Some reported differences may be within run-to-run variation.

The method does not analyze whether the learned insertion order on molecule data corresponds to chemically meaningful substructure order. Unlike the graph task, there is no visualization or quantitative order analysis for molecules, so the mechanistic claim that learned order improves molecule quality remains indirect.

The parameterization is restrictive: a_in = a_um = a is fixed and only b parameters are learned; other CDF families and learned a values are not explored. The closed-form likelihood depends on this special case, and the resulting limitations are not discussed.

The Bregman divergence and loss derivation are not presented intuitively. Eq. 11 mixes a cross-entropy-like term for K^θ with a Bregman term for rates, and the reader must trust Appendix D.4 despite its notational errors. A clearer derivation and ablation of each loss term would strengthen the paper.

strengths: Novel and technically substantive method: the paper injects learnable, data-dependent insertion and unmasking rates into FlexMDM within the DFM framework, showing (Proposition 1) that such rates still generate the desired conditional marginals, and that the order dynamics can be trained jointly with the generator without simulating full trajectories. The Kumaraswamy parameterization with closed-form likelihood and the REINFORCE-leave-one-out + pathwise gradient estimator (single backward pass) are carefully derived and non-trivial.

Strong controlled evidence that the mechanism learns the intended order: on the hard star-graph traversal task, exact match rises from 6.0 (FlexMDM) to 87.9/88.1 for LFlexMDM with a frozen unmasking rate, and the correlation analysis between generation order and distance-from-junction (Figures 4-5) supports that the model learns the locally optimal order.

Meaningful empirical gains on a real task: on de novo molecule generation, validity improves (98.9 -> ~99.7) and quality/validity curves show consistent improvement across sampling budgets (Figure 7 left).

Thorough theoretical appendix: projected DFM construction, projected rate matching as an upper bound on terminal KL (Proposition 5), closed-form Kumaraswamy likelihoods, and a step-by-step gradient derivation.
Reproducibility is reasonable: public datasets (star graphs, SAFE/ZINC), described architecture (DDiT/RoPE/AdaLN), hyperparameter tables, and a code link.
weaknesses: The headline claim of 'learnable order dynamics' is partially self-undermining. The paper's own ablation shows that making the unmasking rate trainable destabilizes training and must be frozen (b_um = 1); in the best configurations only the insertion rate is learned, and unmasking order is elicited post-hoc via confidence selection. The abstract/introduction oversell what is actually learned.

The molecule-quality comparison appears confounded with the diversity-quality tradeoff. At matched diversity (p = 1.0), LFlexMDM quality (~39-43) is essentially identical to FlexMDM (39.5); the headline quality gains (up to ~62) only appear when diversity is reduced via nucleus sampling, and no FlexMDM operating point at matched diversity is provided. The abstract's 'significant improvements in validity and quality' therefore overstates what the evidence supports.

Baseline asymmetry and instability: FlexMDM with confidence-based selection collapses (validity 86.5, uniqueness 20.2, quality 5.8) with no explanation, while several LFlexMDM rows use confidence selection; the comparison conflates confidence-based selection, nucleus truncation p, and the learned rates, making it hard to attribute gains to the proposed mechanism.
No comparison against other insertion-based baselines (e.g., ILM, EditFlows) on molecule generation; only FlexMDM and prior fixed-window models are considered.

Presentation is poor: garbled/misaligned tables (Table 1 columns 'bem/bin', Table 2 appears to drop the quality column and disagrees with Appendix Table 7), duplicated table captions ('Table 5. Hyperparameters for star graphs experiments' twice), figure-caption mismatch for Figure 3, typos ('the dependencies in the tokens is are more global', 'simultaneous simultaneous'), and a garbled description of the diversity-quality result ('50% vs 60%'). These make the central quantitative claims hard to verify.

The strongest quantitative evidence (star graphs) is a synthetic task with a known local optimum and is reported without error bars; combined with the observation that freezing b_um matters more than learning b_in, part of the large gain may stem from training stability rather than order learning per se.
The variance and sample-efficiency of the REINFORCE-LOO estimator with only n = 2 samples is neither analyzed nor ablated, despite being central to the claimed efficiency of joint training.

strengths: The paper introduces a novel framework for learning data-dependent insertion and unmasking rates in variable-length discrete flow matching, enabling learnable generation order without requiring full trajectory simulation.

The theoretical derivation of target rates via Kumaraswamy schedules and the REINFORCE leave-one-out gradient estimator is sound and yields an efficient training procedure with a single backward pass.
On the star graph traversal task, the method convincingly learns the known optimal generation order, achieving a large exact-match improvement over FlexMDM (e.g., 87.9% vs 6.0% on hard).
The molecule generation experiments show promising improvements in validity and quality, with a thoughtful analysis of the diversity-quality trade-off.
The appendix provides extensive derivations, ablations (flexibility vs stability, shared vs separate backbones), and additional results that support the main claims.
weaknesses: The manuscript suffers from numerous presentation issues: typos ('the dependencies in the tokens is are more global', 'simultaneous simultaneous'), inconsistent notation, and mislabeled table headers (e.g., 'bam/bm', 'bem/bin') that make the results difficult to parse.
The 'Quality' metric for molecule generation is never defined, which hampers reproducibility and the interpretation of the reported improvements.

The comparison to FlexMDM is confounded by inference-time sampling parameters: the main table reports FlexMDM only at p=1.0 while LFlexMDM is shown with lower nucleus p and confidence selection. The trade-off plot (Fig. 7 right) may address this, but the text does not clearly explain the matching procedure, so the central claim that learned order dynamics causes the improvement is not fully isolated.

The method only learns the insertion rate; the unmasking rate must be frozen (b_um=1) to avoid training instability. This reduces the scope of 'learnable order dynamics' and the schedule regularization is ad-hoc without ablation on its hyperparameters.

The empirical evaluation is limited to a synthetic graph traversal task and molecule generation; there is no evaluation on text or other sequence domains, and no comparison to related insertion-based models such as EditFlows or ILM.
There is no limitations section, and the impact statement is minimal; potential dual-use concerns of molecule generation are not discussed.
Reproducibility is weakened by the absence of a code link, mislabeled hyperparameter tables (Tables 4 and 5 have swapped captions), and the undefined quality metric.
